doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Music's emotional effect and jazz as foundation
summary: He argues emotional response unites all genres, jazz musicians are eclectic, and Herbie Hancock was his model.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: emotional response — emotional responses, although in varying degrees, from being very subtle to almost like crazy. But still the emotional responses are pretty much the same, whether it’s adulation or whether it’s a joy or sadness, a tear, jumping up crazy, whatever, a big smile on your face, whatever. It’s a fact that whether Samuel Barber “Adagio for Strings” or John Coltrane doing “Greensleeves” or Duke Ellington doing “Satin Doll,” or Aretha Franklin doing “A Natural Woman,” you know, or Al Green doing “Let’s Stay Together,” okay or Jimi Hendrix doing “Hey Joe,” the emotional response is still the same. And we spend so much time separating the music. I think jazz is the music that is the foundation for everything to me. Because I feel that a jazz musician has instinctively more eclectic taste than a rock musician or a classical musician or a country & western musician. Most of the composers in the sixties for Universal Studios especially were primarily jazz musicians. Benny Golson, Benny Carter, Quincy Jones, Oliver Nelson, Lalo Schifrin, Neal Hefti, Gil Melle, Henry Mancini, Nelson Riddle, Marty Paich — all jazz musicians. We didn’t see Aaron Copland in there Okay? We didn’t see Earl Scruggs. You know, whatever. We didn’t see, but we heard classical music. We heard jazz. We heard Rock.

They could write anything you see. So I felt good about that I was part of that community that had, again, those eclectic tastes. And so I just wanted to continue that. My big idol when I was a teenager was Herbie. Because again, the fact that he was with Miles and then doing all these like CTI, and them dates, with Wes Montgomery and people like Paul Desmond. I said I want to do that. That’s what I want to do. He’s playing all this hip stuff over here and then working with Miles, and then doing his own albums. That’s what I wanted to do. But I also made a decision that I wanted to be a producer. I wanted to be a songwriter. I wanted to be a pianist, okay, I wanted to be an arranger. Okay? And I haven’t done a whole host of things as compared to somebody like Randy Brecker or Herbie. But the body of work that I’ve done I really feel proud of, for the fact that it’s been recognized and it’s stood the test of time. So in ’86, I’m moving along right over some stuff.
